newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim rejects striker demands, backs law.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim rejects striker demands, backs law.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam on Tuesday rejected demands by striking workers to scrap a controversial new labour bill, declaring "it is not an evil law".

Kim threw his weight behind the legislation at a news conference and gave no indication he would compromise with militant unions who had threatened to escalate industrial action unless the president backed down.
Kim also ruled out a meeting with opposition parties to try to resolve the crisis.
Hospital workers and unionists at four big television broadcasters on Tuesday joined snowballing strikes that have brought production of cars and ships to a virtual standstill.
"It is not an evil law. It is a necessary one," Kim said, adding that it "will provide a significant impetus for improved competitiveness".
The new law makes the labour market more flexible by allowing employers to lay off workers, hire temporary staff and replace strikers.
"There have been a lot of misunderstandings among the Korean people about this labour law. We have had it for 43 years and it hasn't changed," Kim said.

"Nobody will wear clothes from 43 years ago. We need a labour law that meets the standards of advanced countries. Both employers and workers might be disenchanted with the law but we all need to persevere."

Kim's hardline stand follows a summons by state prosecutors to leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions on Monday to appear for questioning over the strikes, which have been declared illegal.

Employers have threatened to sue union heads for production losses caused by the strikes, which erupted the day the new bill was rammed through parliament on December 26 with no debate and no opposition deputies present.
The main oppostion National Congress for New Politics condemned Kim's comments.
"He showed no responsibility or repentance over the economic crisis or the labour strikes. He has given up his responsibility to govern," a party statement said.
On Tuesday the government put total losses from the industrial unrest so far at 1.18 trillion won ($1.4 billion), including $244 million in lost export earnings.
"If the Republic is to overcome current economic difficulties, labour and management must establish more productive relations in a spirit of participation and cooperation," Kim said.
"We should all share the pain of coping with the difficulties facing industry...thus tiding over the current predicament."
The confederation said 217,000 workers were on strike on Tuesday, up from 190,000 on Monday.
Some 15,000 nurses and orderlies at 24 hospitals resumed stoppages, leaving only emergency care.

"Unless the government withdraws the labour law we will strike indefinitely," declared Kim You-mee, an official at the Korean Federation of Hospital Workers' Unions. Stoppages would be extended to 43 hospitals by Friday, she said.
"We have been threatened with force by the government but if that happens we will only intensify our strikes."
Some 8,000 workers at four broadcasters, including state-run Korea Bradcasting System, walked out early on Tuesday morning, a union official said.

"Non-union workers are putting together programmes at the moment, but we expect some problems with news production later in the day and with production of dramas if the strike continues much longer," Choo Ji-young said.
